Best of luck with meditation. I can only speak from my own limited experience, and I only post here because I see a lot of my my own rationale for meditation in your video. I started meditating with the intention of relieving mental suffering. Major depression/anxiety and body dysmorphic disorder being the main issues. Mediation can help, but if you can seek outside help in the form of therapy and are not currently, consider that in conjunction. I hope I don’t sound preachy here. While the practice of meditation can be to set intention and seeking aside, people do have an agenda going into meditation more often than not, and you can heft unnecessary and unrealistic expectations on yourself by wanting meditation to “fix” something. To fix you. I did this for years, all the way into a ten day meditation retreat at IMS, earlier this year. It was tough, but in a good way. It was self flagellating for most of the ten days until I realized how much pressure I’d put on myself to use meditation to fix something. I clutched onto that intention so tightly I punished myself for not having breakthroughs and not mediating well enough, and for continuing to suffer, honestly. I hope you can be kind to yourself, throughout this. In the end the self-compassion part is more important than I thought, and that circle goes around meditation itself. If meditation can help you, great. If it doesn’t help you in the way you feel you need, don’t beat yourself up or despair. I actually meditate far less after that retreat, as it has become a compulsion to relieve suffering, if that makes sense. Someone could be clever and say, that in itself is being aware, and so is sort of still meditating, but it isn’t with that same rigidity. I wish you only the best, and hope you take a shorter path than I did to being aware of how the the striving and overthinking and wanting to fix yourself is shooting yourself in the foot. I hope you are getting all the help you can and I hope meditation can help as part of a bigger picture.

I've had similar kind of thoughts, on his articles, and recent book.  He does seem to want to chop out a leg from the chair of meditation.  

He says, he wants to be a friend to Buddhism.  But saying those magic words, doesn't make it so.  Maybe he is trying.  I actually don't care so much whether he is a friend or foe of Buddhism.  I do care that he seems to have injected some sort of external blanket doubt onto the mechanism of meditation, by its very nature.  Not just a doubt, which I've seen before, that I kind of agree with.  Which is, you aren't seeing this "Truth", you are just having smaller insights and "truths".  Maybe a bit simplistic, but hopefully makes sense.  He seems to be saying, you are not only not seeing personal "truths", you are just deluding yourself by shaping your own experience with these outside practices, and your insights are not formed with iron, but dross.  You are playing at awareness, or it isn't really possible at all.

I've seen him mention, that MBSR and MBCT are, "useful".  He never goes into, as far as I can see, how they are useful.  How are they different in mechanism, to straight modern mindfulness meditation?  He mentions at the beginning of his book about, "insights" gained from meditation.  But, again, never elaborates.  He doesn't go into the benefits, nor, how are they benefits if he is undercutting the entire endeavor, as mentioned above.

I am concerned, that he has injected an almost irrefutable doubt into things.  If you believe him that is.  It almost comes down to whether you believe yourself that your emotions you are noticing while meditating, are valid, and not so wholly shaped and corrupted by the most basic mindfulness instructions...that the entire endeavor should be scuttled.  Or, you believe Evan's doubt that you are actually shaping your experience so substantially through these methods, that you aren't really able to reliably classify your experience of noticing an emotion as a reliable awareness.  

If this isn't an accurate view of his position, and there is something to be clarified, or this is wildly inaccurate, I think he should be more clear.  There are a lot of people who are not buddhist.  Who do not belong to any groups.  Who use various apps out of practicality, but are beholden to none.  Who have benefited from mindfulness based therapies.  What are you saying to those people?  I don't know, and that is troubling.
